issues.legal_issue: A judgment determining that rent could be assessed does not bar a later determination of whether the tenancy is permanent when the earlier proceeding did not put the character of the tenancy directly or substantially in issue.
material_facts: An earlier proceeding concerned whether rent could be assessed for the land and, if so, at what rate.
The earlier proceeding resulted in an increase in rent, but its issues did not include whether the tenancy was permanent and heritable.
The later proceeding was an ejectment suit in which the tenant relied on the tenancy being permanent and heritable.
The provision under which rent was assessed did not make rent assessment depend on the tenancy being non-permanent.
issues.conclusion: The earlier rent-assessment decision did not operate as res judicata on the question of permanency of the tenure.
issues.legal_principle: A matter is not barred by res judicata when it was not directly or substantially in issue in the earlier proceeding. Permanency of tenure does not necessarily entail fixed rent, and an enhancement of rent does not necessarily negate permanency. The Court relied on Shankarrao v. Sambhu Wallad (1940) 45 C.W.N. 57, applying that principle to an agricultural tenancy, and its application to non-agricultural tenancies in Jogendra Krishna Banerji v. Subashini Dassi (1940) 45 C.W.N. 590 and Probhas Chandra Mallik v. Debendra Nath Das (1939) 43 C.W.N. 828. The earlier rent assessment had been made under sections 9 and 10 of Regulation V of 1812, which did not make assessment conditional on the tenancy being non-permanent.

predicates.later_ejectment_proceeding: A landlord brings a later proceeding seeking to eject a tenant and the tenant's tenure is in dispute.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_only_decided_rent_ass: An earlier proceeding decided whether rent could be assessed and, if so, its amount.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_put_tenure_character_: The earlier proceeding directly or substantially considered whether the tenure was permanent.

issues.definition: When an ejectment proceeding follows an earlier proceeding limited to rent assessment that did not directly or substantially consider permanency, the earlier assessment does not bar deciding permanency in the later proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A permanent and heritable tenancy may be inferred from the cumulative effect of long-standing possession, successive transfers, permanent improvements, stable rent, and the landlords' conduct.
material_facts: The origin and original nature of the earliest known tenancy were unknown.
The tenancy passed through inheritance, wills, and transfers between living persons, and transfer deeds described enjoyment as continuing to successors for generations.
A tank, masonry steps, walls, and substantial buildings were constructed on the land; bricks were also made from its earth, and mortgages were executed against the property.
Rent was increased in an earlier period but remained unchanged thereafter.
Landlords accepted rent from transferees or successors and did not seek ejectment or further rent enhancement despite increases in land value and letting value.
The later proceeding was a landlord's suit to eject the tenant.
issues.conclusion: The cumulative circumstances irresistibly established that the tenancy was permanent and heritable, so the landlord's claim for ejectment was rightly dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Possession for generations at a uniform rent, or construction of permanent structures, is not by itself conclusive proof of a permanent tenancy; the cumulative effect of those circumstances together with other facts may support that inference. The Court relied on Probhas Chandra Mallik v. Debendra Nath Das (1939) 43 C.W.N. 828. It distinguished the fact-specific decisions in Rasmoy Purkatt v. Srinath Moyra, 7 C.W.N. 132; Digbijoy Roy v. Shaikh Aya Rahman, 17 C.W.N. 156; Satyendra Nath v. Charu Sankar, 40 C.W.N. 854; and Kamal Kumar Datta v. Nanda Lal Dule, (1929) I.L.R. 56 Cal. 738.

rule.if: ejectment_proceeding and earliest_tenancy_origin_unknown and tenancy_passed_through_successions_or_transfers and transfer_deeds_described_generational_enjoyment and permanent_improvements_were_made and rent_remained_stable_after_increase and landlords_accepted_rent_from_successors and landlords_did_not_seek_ejectment_or_further_increase_despite_rising_values

predicates.ejectment_proceeding: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking to eject a tenant.
predicates.earliest_tenancy_origin_unknown: The evidence does not establish how the earliest known tenant acquired the tenancy or what its original nature was.
predicates.tenancy_passed_through_successions_or_tr: The tenancy passed from one holder to another by inheritance, will, or transfer between living persons.
predicates.transfer_deeds_described_generational_en: Deeds transferring the tenancy described the transferee's enjoyment as continuing to later generations.
predicates.permanent_improvements_were_made: The tenant or successive holders constructed lasting works or substantial buildings on the land.
predicates.rent_remained_stable_after_increase: After an earlier increase, the rent continued at the same level.
predicates.landlords_accepted_rent_from_successors: The landlords accepted rent from persons who succeeded to or acquired the tenancy.
predicates.landlords_did_not_seek_ejectment_or_furt: Despite increased land or letting values, the landlords neither sought to eject the tenant nor sought a further rent increase.

issues.definition: When an ejectment proceeding involves an unexplained tenancy origin together with successive transfers, deeds providing for generational enjoyment, lasting improvements, stable rent, and the landlords' continued acceptance of rent without ejectment or further increase despite rising values, the tenancy is inferred to be permanent and heritable.
